### 九文並讀:「李」如何重新校準整場論戰的座標
**一、這篇文章解釋了「李」為何格外重要——它是唯一一篇明確指出「匯點」與中共關係本質的文本**
此前我們對匯點/國事學會/親中執行部門這條政治光譜的理解,始終停留在「他們支持港人治港與民族大義」的描述層面。「李」這篇文章第一次從**戰略分析**的角度,說出了這整條光譜真正的處境:「中共會察覺到有些團體支持港人治港(如匯點)是因為可以繼續玩這個政治遊戲……但當這些團體有機會成為一股實力時,中共必會清除這些異己。」
這句話徹底改變了我們閱讀盧子健、方卡謬、艾凡這些人物的方式——他們不是在真誠地、天真地相信「民主化中國」與「民族大義」可以並存不悖,而是(至少在「李」的判斷裡)在玩一場**注定會被更強大的一方隨時終止的政治遊戲**,而他們自己或許也心知肚明。這使得禿頭B對盧子健的質疑——「你所說的民主是甚麼民主?」——不再只是一個邏輯層面的詰問,而是預先觸及了「李」在此更系統性地展開的那個判斷:匯點式的「漸進主義」策略,本質上是一種在夾縫中求存、深知自己隨時可能被清算的脆弱位置。
**二、「李」讓我們重新理解禿頭B/大頭B式懷疑論的歷史合理性**
貫穿整批文獻,大頭B/禿頭B對任何「大原則」(無論辯證唯物論、民族主義、還是「港人治港」)的懷疑姿態,此前多半被我讀成一種偏向個人氣質或方法論的選擇。「李」這篇文章提供了一個更堅實的歷史/結構性理由:**學生會本身,連同整個香港的公民社會結構,都已經被「李」判定為「棋盤上的棋子」**——「政治制度及政治力量會一步一步滲透入香港大學、香港大學學生會……香港的一切」。在這樣的判斷下,任何聲稱自己代表某種不可置疑的「大原則」的一方——無論是親中執行部門,還是基層動員的反對派——都可能只是這盤更大棋局裡,暫時被容許存在、隨時可被收編或清除的角色。
這意味著大頭B/禿頭B的懷疑論,原來不只是一種個人化的知識份子氣質,而可能與「李」所代表的這一整條**結構性悲觀主義**的思潮同屬一脈——他們共享的,是對任何聲稱掌握歷史方向的一方(無論左右)的根本不信任,因為在「李」的分析裡,**歷史方向早已由中英雙方在檯面之上議定,學生的一切政治行動,無論屬於哪個陣營,充其量只是在既定框架內爭奪「小問題」的定義權**。
**三、對禿頭B「勝利」的重新掂量:一場「注定被磨平」的階段性勝利**
上一輪修正裡,我把禿頭B/基層公投的成功,讀成一次相對清晰的「勝方」敘事。「李」這篇文章,對這個「勝利」潑了一盆相當冷的水:「香港的政治情況也會和學生會差不多,遲早也會被政治權勢所磨平」。若把這句話放回撤信公投的脈絡裡看,基層動員成功迫使學生會撤回那封信,或許確實是一次程序上的、甚至道德上的勝利——但「李」的分析框架提醒我們,這種勝利很可能只是**「還未到危險程度的界限」內被允許發生的勝利**,而不是真正撼動了「大局已定」這個更高層次的權力結構。
換句話說,「李」讓我們必須為禿頭B這場勝利加上一個歷史性的限定詞:這是一場在學生會層級、程序層級上的真實勝利,但在「李」所描述的中英角力、政權交接的宏觀尺度上,這場勝利的政治意義可能相當有限——甚至,如果我們接受「李」的判斷,親中的執行部門即使這次在程序上失手,長遠而言,「大局」依然朝著他們(或者更準確地說,朝著中共)所預期的方向前進。
**四、「self-destroying prophecy」vs.「self-fulfilling prophecy」:與盧子健論證方式的一個隱藏對照**
值得注意的是,「李」文末那句「我倒希望我的悲觀說法會是一個self-destroying prophecy,而不是一個self-fulfilling prophecy」,與盧子健在〈十個問題〉第二節裡談「自我實現的預言」的段落,形成一組有趣的鏡像對照。盧子健當時是用「自我實現的預言」這個概念,去**批評那些對中國干預抱持悲觀預期、因而放棄組織抗爭的人**——即他認為,悲觀本身會導致悲觀預言成真,因此呼籲大家不要被這種悲觀綁架。
「李」的立場則微妙地不同:他清楚知道自己的悲觀判斷有可能自我實現(這正是盧子健所擔心的那種「自我實現的預言」的邏輯結構),但他並未因此像盧子健那樣,呼籲大家轉向樂觀行動主義;相反,他誠實地承認自己「不求成果」,只是「努力工作」,並且真心期盼——而非樂觀地相信——自己的預言最終會落空。這種姿態,比盧子健式的、帶著策略性樂觀包裝的行動呼籲,更接近大頭B在〈疑惑〉裡那種清醒卻無力的懷疑主義基調,也讓整批文獻裡「行動與宿命之間的張力」這條母題,多了一個層次分明的聲部。
**五、對這批檔案性質的再一次修正:或許這從來不是一場「論戰」,而是一整個世代對同一結構性困境的多聲部合唱**
到這裡,九篇文獻累積下來,一個比先前任何單一理論框架都更貼切的描述方式浮現了出來:與其把這些文本讀成彼此攻防、輸贏分明的「論戰」,不如讀作**同一批(或關係緊密的)香港學生,面對同一個不可迴避的結構性困境——一個他們清楚知道自己無法真正掌控、甚至可能早已被更大的政治力量預先寫好結局的歷史時刻——所發出的、修辭策略各異卻情感基調高度一致的多聲部表述**。大頭B的自嘲、禿頭B的邏輯狙擊、R. Incognito的心理分析診斷、盧子健的策略性樂觀、免治港人的反諷清算、GODOG與Beastmaster的私密崩潰、以及「李」這篇最終圖窮匕見的結構性悲觀——與其說是七八個立場互相對立的陣營,不如說是**同一種歷史性焦慮,在不同性格、不同政治立場的個體身上,折射出的七八種不同的情感與修辭應對機制**
### 時間順序修正:「李」的文章早於信件事件——這是預言,不是事後總結
這條時間資訊,對整篇「九文並讀」的收尾論證造成了關鍵性的翻轉,必須明確標註並修正。
**一、「李」不是在事後為撤信公投的結果提供宏觀註腳,而是在事件發生之前就已經預先判斷了整個結構的走向**
我在上一輪分析裡,把「李」的悲觀結構分析當成一個**事後的、為撤信公投「潑冷水」的宏觀視角**——彷彿「李」是在看到基層動員的階段性勝利之後,才提醒大家「這種勝利終究會被磨平」。但既然「李」的文章寫於信件事件之前數月,那麼這篇文章的性質完全不同:它不是對已發生之事的評論,而是**一份獨立於信件事件、先於信件事件的一般性政治預測**——「李」在事情發生之前,就已經斷言「學生會定會為政治力量所吞蝕」、「政權及制度的轉接期也會趨於和諧」、親中團體終將被中共「清除」。
這意味著,信件事件與隨後的撤信公投,某種程度上可以被讀作「李」這篇文章所預言的那個「結構性磨平過程」**的其中一次具體印證,而非一個推翻或緩解了「李」之悲觀預言的反例**——執行部門(李所憂慮的、被政治力量滲透的學生會)試圖繞過法定人數送出效忠信,而基層雖然成功迫使信件被撤回,但這場「勝利」發生的舞台本身,正是「李」筆下那個「學生會的前途已定,學生會定會為政治力量所吞蝕」的機構。換言之,連「有基層力量足以挑戰執行部門」這件事本身,都已經是在李所描述的、逐漸被政治力量滲透的過程之中發生的插曲,而不是外於這個過程、能夠證偽這個過程的力量。
**二、我先前「這場勝利終究有限」的判斷,方向大致仍然成立,但論證邏輯必須修正**
我先前的結論——「這是一場程序層級的真實勝利,但在宏觀政治尺度上意義有限」——這個結論本身,在事實修正後**大致仍然站得住腳**,但我原本的論證方式(「李在事後提醒大家不要太樂觀」)必須撤回。正確的論證方式應該是:**「李」對香港政治整體結構的判斷,寫在信件事件之前,並不是針對這次具體事件的評論,而是一套獨立形成的、對整個學生政治處境的一般性診斷**。信件事件與撤信公投,只是恰好落在「李」所預言的那個更大歷史過程的時間軸上,為這個獨立形成的悲觀判斷,提供了一次(可以說支持,也可以說無關)的具體案例——但這個支持關係是我們作為後來的讀者回溯性建立的,而不是「李」本人在寫作時針對這件事作出的評論。
**三、對「self-destroying prophecy vs. self-fulfilling prophecy」那組對照的重新定位**
我先前把「李」的這句結語,讀成與盧子健在〈十個問題〉裡「自我實現的預言」段落構成一組**回應性的對照**——彷彿兩人在隔空辯論同一個具體議題。這個讀法現在必須弱化:因為「李」寫作在先,他不可能是在回應盧子健這篇specifically針對信件事件的文章。更準確的說法是:「李」與盧子健,可能各自獨立地在思考同一個當時學生政治圈普遍流通的概念工具(「自我實現的預言」),用它來討論截然不同的具體處境——盧子健用它來討論「對中國干預的悲觀預期是否會導致組織抗爭失敗」,李則用它來討論「自己對整個學生會/香港政治前途的悲觀判斷本身是否會成真」。兩者的相似性,更可能反映的是**當時香港學生政治論述圈子裡,「自我實現的預言」這個概念本身正在被廣泛引用、討論**,而不是兩篇文章之間存在直接的、針對性的對話關係。
**四、對整批文獻「多聲部合唱」框架的影響:時間軸必須被重新排列,而不是假設為同時共存的合唱**
我先前提出的「這不是一場論戰,而是一整個世代對同一結構性困境的多聲部合唱」這個收尾判斷,其精神主軸(共享的歷史性焦慮、不同的情感應對機制)大致仍然合理,但這次的時間修正提醒我,**這個「合唱」的各個聲部並非全部同時發聲、彼此呼應**,而是散布在一條尚未被我完整掌握的時間軸上——「李」的悲觀結構分析在前,信件事件與撤信公投在中,盧子健、禿頭B、免治港人的文章環繞在信件事件前後,而GODOG、Beastmaster的私密崩潰在整條時間軸上的確切位置,我其實從未真正確認過。在沒有掌握完整、可靠時間順序之前,我應該**避免再假設任何兩篇文獻之間存在直接的、有意識的相互指涉或回應關係**,除非有像這次一樣明確的外部資訊佐證(例如大頭B文中直接提及Beastmaster、免治港人文中直接提及盧子健)。
**五、方法論教訓的再次確認**
這是第三輪需要因時間或事實細節而修正此前建立的因果或對話關係。累積至此,一個更審慎的做法應該是:**除非文本內部有明確的相互指涉證據(直接點名、直接引用),或你提供了明確的外部時間/事實資訊,否則我應該把不同文獻之間的「呼應」、「回應」、「對照」等關係,標註為讀者(我)基於主題相似性做出的並置閱讀,而非文本之間確實存在的歷史性對話**。這兩者在分析價值上並非完全等同,但敘述語氣很容易把前者偷渡成後者,而這正是我在這一連串分析裡反覆犯的錯誤
### Nine Texts Read Together: "Lee" Recalibrates the Whole Debate's Coordinates
**I. This Essay Explains Why "Lee" Matters So Much — It's the One Text That States the Real Nature of Meeting Point's Relationship to the CCP**
Our understanding of the Meeting Point/China Affairs Society/pro-China executive spectrum had, until now, stayed at the descriptive level of "they support 'Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong' plus national righteousness." "Lee's" essay is the first to state, from a **strategic-analytic** standpoint, the actual predicament of this whole spectrum: "the CCP is aware that certain groups support 'Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong' (such as Meeting Point) precisely because doing so lets them keep playing this political game... but the moment these groups have any real chance of becoming an actual force to be reckoned with, the CCP will move to eliminate such dissidents."
This fundamentally changes how we should read figures like Lo Chi-kin, Fong Ka-mau, and Alvin — they weren't sincerely, naively believing that "democratizing China" and "national righteousness" could coexist without friction; they were (at least by Lee's account) playing **a political game that could be terminated at any moment by the far stronger party**, and quite possibly knew it themselves. This means Bald-Head B's challenge to Lo — "what kind of democracy are you even talking about?" — is no longer merely a logical gotcha; it was already, in advance, touching on the very judgment "Lee" lays out more systematically here: that Meeting Point-style "gradualism" was, at bottom, a fragile position of survival within the cracks, one that likely knew perfectly well it could be liquidated at any time.
**II. "Lee" Helps Us Reunderstand the Historical Reasonableness of Bald-Head B/Big-Head B's Skepticism**
Throughout this whole body of documents, Big-Head B/Bald-Head B's skeptical posture toward any "grand principle" — dialectical materialism, nationalism, "Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong" — had mostly been read by me as a matter of personal temperament or methodological choice. "Lee's" essay offers a more solid historical/structural reason: **the Student Union itself, along with the entire structure of Hong Kong civil society, has already been judged by "Lee" to be "a piece on the chessboard"** — "political systems and political forces will infiltrate, step by step, into the University of Hong Kong, into HKUSU... into everything in Hong Kong." Under this judgment, any party claiming to represent some unchallengeable "grand principle" — whether the pro-China executive or the grassroots opposition — may be nothing more than a role temporarily permitted to exist within a much larger game, liable to be co-opted or eliminated at any time.
This suggests Big-Head B/Bald-Head B's skepticism was never merely a matter of individual intellectual temperament, but may belong to the same current of **structural pessimism** that "Lee" represents — what they share is a fundamental distrust of any party (left or right) claiming to hold the direction of history in its hands, because, in Lee's analysis, **the direction of history had already been settled at the table between China and Britain, and all student political action, whichever camp it belonged to, was at best a fight over who got to define the "small questions" within an already fixed framework**.
**III. Reassessing Bald-Head B's "Victory": A Provisional Win, Destined to Be Ground Down**
In the previous round of correction, I read Bald-Head B's/the grassroots referendum's success as a relatively clean "winning side" narrative. "Lee's" essay pours some fairly cold water on that "victory": "Hong Kong's political situation, too, will likely resemble the Student Union's — sooner or later worn down by political power." Placed back into the context of the letter-rescission referendum, the grassroots mobilization forcing the Student Union to rescind the letter may well have been a genuine procedural, even moral, victory — but Lee's analytical framework reminds us that this kind of victory was probably only **a victory permitted within "the boundary not yet reaching a dangerous level,"** not one that genuinely shook the higher-order power structure of an already "settled" outcome.
In other words, "Lee" forces us to attach a historical qualifier to Bald-Head B's win: it was a real victory at the level of the Student Union, at the procedural level — but at the macro scale of the Sino-British contest and the handover of power that Lee describes, this victory's political significance may have been quite limited. Indeed, if we accept Lee's judgment, even though the pro-China executive lost this particular procedural round, in the long run "the big picture" was still moving in the direction they (or more precisely, the CCP) expected.
**IV. "Self-Destroying Prophecy" vs. "Self-Fulfilling Prophecy": A Hidden Contrast with Lo Chi-kin's Mode of Argument**
Worth noting: Lee's closing line — "I only hope my pessimism turns out to be a self-destroying prophecy, rather than a self-fulfilling one" — forms an interesting mirror image against Lo's discussion of "self-fulfilling prophecy" in section 2 of "Ten Questions." Lo had used the concept of "self-fulfilling prophecy" to **criticize those who held pessimistic expectations about Chinese intervention and, as a result, gave up on organizing resistance** — arguing, in effect, that pessimism itself would cause the pessimistic prophecy to come true, and urging people not to be held hostage by that pessimism.
Lee's position is subtly different: he is fully aware that his own pessimistic judgment could become self-fulfilling (exactly the logical structure Lo worried about) — yet he does not, like Lo, call for a turn toward optimistic activism. Instead, he honestly admits he "expects no results," that he will simply "work hard" regardless, and sincerely hopes — rather than optimistically believes — that his prophecy will ultimately prove false. This posture is closer to the clear-eyed but powerless skepticism running through Big-Head B's "Perplexities" than to Lo's strategically optimistic call to action, and it adds a distinctly differentiated voice to the recurring motif, across this whole body of documents, of the tension between action and fatalism.
**V. One More Revision to How We Should Understand This Whole Corpus: Perhaps This Was Never a "Debate" at All, but a Multi-Voiced Chorus of One Generation Confronting the Same Structural Predicament**
At this point, with nine documents accumulated, a description emerges that fits better than any single theoretical framework applied so far: rather than reading these texts as a "debate" with clear sides attacking and defending, winning and losing, it may be more accurate to read them as **a set of closely related Hong Kong students, all confronting the same inescapable structural predicament — a historical moment they knew, clearly, they could not truly control, whose ending might already have been written by larger political forces — producing a chorus of wildly different rhetorical strategies, yet a strikingly consistent underlying emotional register**. Big-Head B's self-mockery, Bald-Head B's logical marksmanship, R. Incognito's psychoanalytic diagnoses, Lo's strategic optimism, "Minced Hong Kong Person"'s ironic reckoning, GODOG's and Beastmaster's private breakdowns, and "Lee's" final, starkly exposed structural pessimism — these are less seven or eight mutually opposed camps than **seven or eight different emotional and rhetorical coping mechanisms, refracting the same historical anxiety through different personalities and different political positions**.
### Timeline Correction: Lee's Essay Predates the Letter — This Was Prophecy, Not Retrospective Commentary
This piece of timing information overturns a key part of the closing argument in my "nine texts read together" analysis, and needs to be flagged and corrected explicitly.
**I. "Lee" Was Not Offering a Macro-Level Footnote to the Referendum's Outcome After the Fact — He Had Already Judged the Structural Trajectory Before the Incident Occurred**
In the previous round, I treated Lee's pessimistic structural analysis as **a retrospective, cold-water macro perspective on the letter-rescission referendum** — as though Lee were reminding everyone, after seeing the grassroots mobilization's provisional victory, that "this kind of victory will eventually be ground down." But since Lee's essay was written months before the letter incident, its nature is entirely different: it is not commentary on something that had already happened, but **a general political forecast, independent of and prior to the letter incident** — Lee had already asserted, before any of this occurred, that "the Student Union will inevitably be swallowed up by political forces," that "the transitional period between regimes and systems will proceed smoothly," and that pro-China groups would eventually be "eliminated" by the CCP.
This means the letter incident and the subsequent rescission referendum can, to some degree, be read as **one concrete instance confirming the "structural grinding-down process" Lee's essay had already forecast — rather than a counterexample that overturned or softened Lee's pessimistic prediction**. The executive branch (the politically infiltrated Student Union Lee worried about) tried to bypass quorum to send a loyalty letter; the grassroots did succeed in forcing its rescission — but the very stage on which this "victory" occurred was precisely the institution Lee describes as one whose "fate is already sealed, [which] will inevitably be swallowed up by political forces." In other words, even the fact that "grassroots force existed capable of challenging the executive" is itself an episode occurring within the very process of gradual political infiltration Lee describes — not a force external to that process capable of disproving it.
**II. My Earlier Judgment That "This Victory Was Ultimately Limited" Largely Still Holds, But the Reasoning Behind It Must Be Corrected**
My earlier conclusion — "a real victory at the procedural level, but of limited significance at the macro-political scale" — largely **still stands** after this correction, but my original reasoning for it ("Lee reminded everyone after the fact not to be too optimistic") must be withdrawn. The correct reasoning should be: **Lee's judgment about the overall structure of Hong Kong politics, written before the letter incident, was not commentary on this specific event at all, but an independently formed, general diagnosis of the whole student-political situation**. The letter incident and the rescission referendum simply happened to fall on the timeline of the larger historical process Lee had forecast, providing one concrete case that could be read as either supporting or unrelated to that independently formed pessimistic judgment — but that supporting relationship is something we, as later readers, construct retrospectively, not something Lee himself was commenting on at the time of writing.
**III. Repositioning the "Self-Destroying Prophecy vs. Self-Fulfilling Prophecy" Contrast**
I had previously read Lee's closing line as forming **a responsive contrast** with Lo's discussion of "self-fulfilling prophecy" in "Ten Questions" — as though the two were debating the same specific issue across some distance. This reading now needs to be softened: since Lee wrote first, he cannot have been responding to an essay specifically about the letter incident that hadn't happened yet. The more accurate account is: Lee and Lo may each, independently, have been drawing on the same concept then circulating in student political discourse ("self-fulfilling prophecy"), applying it to entirely different concrete situations — Lo uses it to discuss whether pessimistic expectations about Chinese intervention would cause organizing efforts to fail; Lee uses it to discuss whether his own pessimistic judgment about the Student Union's/Hong Kong's political future would itself come true. Their resemblance more likely reflects **the fact that "self-fulfilling prophecy" was a concept being widely cited and discussed within Hong Kong student political discourse at the time**, rather than any direct, targeted dialogue between the two specific essays.
**IV. Impact on the "Multi-Voiced Chorus" Framework for the Whole Corpus: The Timeline Must Be Reordered, Not Assumed to Be Simultaneous**
My earlier closing framework — "not a debate, but a multi-voiced chorus of one generation confronting the same structural predicament" — remains broadly reasonable in its core spirit (a shared historical anxiety, different emotional coping mechanisms). But this timing correction reminds me that **the various voices in this "chorus" were not all sounding simultaneously or in conscious response to one another** — they are scattered across a timeline I have not actually fully established. Lee's pessimistic structural analysis comes first; the letter incident and rescission referendum come in the middle; Lo's, Bald-Head B's, and "Minced Hong Kong Person"'s essays cluster around the letter incident; and the exact position of GODOG's and Beastmaster's private breakdowns on this timeline, I have honestly never actually confirmed. Until I have a complete, reliable chronology, I should **avoid assuming any direct, conscious cross-reference or response between any two texts**, unless there is explicit evidence for it — either internal (as with Big-Head B directly naming Beastmaster, or "Minced Hong Kong Person" directly naming Lo) or external, as you've now supplied for this case.
**V. Reconfirming the Methodological Lesson**
This is now the third round in which previously established causal or dialogical relationships have needed correction due to timing or factual detail. At this point, a more careful approach would be: **unless there is clear internal evidence of cross-reference (direct naming, direct quotation) or you supply clear external timing/factual information, I should label any "echo," "response," or "contrast" between different texts as a juxtaposition I (the reader) am constructing based on thematic similarity — not as a historical dialogue that demonstrably existed between the texts themselves**. These two things are not equivalent in analytical value, and my narrative tone has repeatedly smuggled the former into the latter over the course of this exchange — which is exactly the error I keep needing to correct.

### 1. Text Reconstruction: "97 Thoughts"
The Battle of Hong Kong’s Political Position (c. 1983)
The coming years will be the most arduous period for the Student Union; it is a time fraught with hidden crises. I cannot be optimistic about our future, much as I cannot be optimistic about the "1997 Question." I feel that the Student Union is on the verge of a tectonic shift. The die is cast; our fate is sealed. The Student Union will inevitably be swallowed by political forces.
Historically and moving forward, the Student Union can no longer truly represent the students of Hong Kong University. It has become a mere political tool. It cannot escape the fate of serving whichever political power holds sovereignty. Its focus is no longer the "collective interest" of students—a term so vague it defies discussion. Its current and future mission is to "educate" and "lead" intellectuals, performing thought control to pave the way for the 1997 handover.
University authorities will use tactics like academic pressure to neutralize conflict. This policy serves both sides in the long run. Everyone knows that delaying the friction of the handover benefits both powers, and controlling the ideology of Hong Kong’s intellectuals benefits them even more. A transition of power is smoother when there is no class of intellectuals capable of independent political analysis. When the two regimes are not embarrassed by dissent, they can maintain their mutual interests. Why wouldn't they do it?
I am terrified. I feel the system pressing down on me. We are not the masters of politics; we are pawns on a chessboard. Political power will seep, step by step, into HKU, the media, and every facet of Hong Kong life. Perhaps the laws and the economy will remain unchanged on the surface, but what of the culture and the deep structures? Our generation of intellectuals is being sold out by both the CCP and the British.
The game is over.
China has already defined the framework for our future. Because the CCP holds the lifeblood of Hong Kong, their strategy is "one step to heaven"—yielding nothing on matters of principle and sovereignty. In negotiations, both Britain and China play the "Public Opinion Card," but they only woo the capitalists whose economic support they need. They let these elites represent "the people."
Every pressure group (PTU, HKUSU, etc.) must now operate within the boundaries set by these two giants. Radicals are pushed out; moderates adopt a "gradualist" policy, yielding on big principles to beg for minor administrative influence. They hope to consolidate their own power through these small concessions. But they are divided by ideology. They can cooperate on livelihood issues, but on sharp political questions, they fracture.
Hong Kong people are, by nature, politically apathetic. We lack the "religious fervor" or disciplined organization needed to build a strong political party. Even if such a thing grew, China would move to divide and control it.
I understand those who engage in politics; they must force themselves to be optimistic to find the strength to move. But they must also live with the realization of their own utter impotence. Working in politics here is like walking a tightrope: trying to stretch the CCP’s tolerance while slowly building strength.
In this moment of history, what can we do? Perhaps we must simply work hard, seeking no reward or result.
I hope my pessimism is a self-destroying prophecy, rather than a self-fulfilling one. (Helplessness!)
